title: BORIS in Hormone-Driven Cancers: Epigenetic Reprogramming, Transcriptional Plasticity, and Therapeutic Implications.
authors: Saleem, Sara; Gaughan, Luke; Robson, Craig N
abstract: Hormone-driven cancers, including prostate, breast, endometrial and ovarian cancers, are a leading cause of cancer-related mortality. Endocrine therapies targeting androgen receptor and oestrogen receptor/progesterone receptor signalling have improved outcomes, but acquired resistance arising through genetic and epigenetic mechanisms that bypass receptor dependence remains a major challenge. BORIS (Brother of the Regulator of Imprinted Sites), a CTCF paralogue, is a germline-restricted regulator that becomes aberrantly reactivated in cancer through promoter hypomethylation, p53 loss, and loss of CTCF-mediated repression. Once expressed, BORIS occupies CTCF sites, displacing or co-occupying them with CTCF, and reprograms clustered sites into alternative transcriptional start sites through SRCAP-mediated H2A.Z deposition, activating germline genes that sustain proliferation, and therapeutic resistance. BORIS expression correlates with poor prognosis in ovarian and endometrial cancers, associates with ER/PR levels in breast cancer, and correlates with Gleason score in prostate cancer. BORIS represses AR signalling in ovarian cancer and inversely correlates with receptor expression in endometrial cancer. Its cancer-testis antigen properties position BORIS as an immunotherapy target, with preclinical vaccine efficacy demonstrated in breast cancer models. This review synthesises the disease-specific evidence positioning BORIS as a driver of transcriptional reprogramming and endocrine resistance, identifies current knowledge gaps, and discusses translational implications of targeting this pathway.

title: CTCF-regulated miR-646 suppresses colorectal cancer progression through Wnt/beta-catenin signaling pathway by targeting WNT2B.
authors: Chen, Gao-Min; Song, Xiao-Hang; Ding, Yi-Han; Dong, Yi; Chen, Bo-Jian; Yang, Xiao; Yu, Wen-Han; Zhang, Kai; Zhang, Xin-Er; Zhang, Run-Qi; Tang, Ya-Nan; Lei, Xue-Tao; Liao, Yi-Jun; Chen, Jing-Song
abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a common malignancy associated with Wnt/beta-catenin pathway dysregulation. While miRNAs are known to influence cancer, miR-646's role in CRC remains unclear. This study employed qPCR, Western blot, IHC, CCK-8, and Transwell assays to assess miR-646 expression, protein levels, and CRC cell functions. Wnt/beta-catenin activation was analyzed using IF, TOP/FOP reporter assays, and gene interactions were examined through ChIP and dual-luciferase systems. Nude mouse models and clinical samples were used to further evaluate the biological and clinical relevance of miR-646 in CRC. Results showed miR-646 was downregulated in CRC. Its upregulation suppressed CRC cell proliferation, migration, and invasion by inhibiting WNT2B and Wnt/beta-catenin activation. CTCF negatively regulated miR-646 expression, potentially through its binding to the miR-646 promoter. In vivo, miR-646 knockdown promoted CRC xenograft tumor growth, accompanied by increased WNT2B expression and enhanced Wnt/beta-catenin signaling. Additionally, higher miR-646 expression was associated with a better prognosis in patients with CRC. These findings support a role for miR-646 in regulating WNT2B/Wnt/beta-catenin signaling in CRC and demonstrate its negative regulation by CTCF, suggesting the potential of miR-646 as a prognostic biomarker and therapeutic target.

title: CTCF regulates wild-type and recombinant AAV gene expression by shaping viral chromatin.
authors: Larsen, Clairine I S; Abrahams, Rhiannon R; Guertler, Rea; Wilion, Elliott M; Erata, Eda; Sykes, Zachary H; Stoica, Lorelei I; Thirumoorthy, Gopishankar; Sinha, Divya; Rai, Richa; Majumder, Joydeb; Hofer, Elizabeth K; Hart, Eleanor; Dissanayake, Eishika; Gern, James E; Gamm, David M; Murphy, William L; Fuller, Matthew S; Majumder, Kinjal
abstract: Adeno-Associated Viruses (AAVs) are powerful platforms for delivering therapeutic transgenes via recombinant AAV (rAAV) vectors. However, a limited understanding of the regulation of AAV gene expression has narrowed the ability to efficiently express therapeutic transgenes from rAAV vectors. Since rAAVs retain only the wtAAV inverted terminal repeats (ITR), we hypothesized that regulatory elements outside the ITR that govern wild-type AAV (wtAAV) gene expression can be used to modify rAAV genomes to enhance vector performance. Through in silico analysis, biochemical pulldowns, and high-throughput sequencing, we have identified that the host architectural protein CCCTC-binding Factor (CTCF) associates with the wtAAV type 2 (wtAAV2) genome but is absent from rAAV vectors. Global knockdown and site-specific deletion revealed that the CTCF binding element (CBE) on the wtAAV2 genome, located upstream of the viral P5 promoter, regulates expression of the viral Rep68/78 genes. We have re-engineered new rAAV vectors expressing a GFP reporter transgene to contain the wtAAV2-CBE upstream of the vector promoter. Our results show that CTCF binding dramatically increased rAAV transduction efficiency and GFP expression by up to four-fold across multiple cell types. This enhancement was independent of the AAV capsid serotype used for packaging rAAV vectors. CUT&RUN analysis revealed that this CBE was necessary and sufficient to regulate the chromatin landscape of wtAAV2 and rAAV2. Finally, we observed that CTCF-mediated chromatin remodeling of rAAV2 led to increased production of nascent RNA transcripts from the vector genome. Based on our findings, we propose that CTCF supports wtAAV2/rAAV gene expression by shaping the local chromatin landscape.

title: Uhrf1 loss disrupts CTCF-associated chromatin organization during early mouse embryogenesis.
authors: Kurowski, Agata; Zhu, Bohan; Sun, Yifei; Sargunas, Paul; Jain, Nimisha; Chan, Ashley; Hadri, Lahouaria; Shi, Yi; Walsh, Martin J; Ma, Sai
abstract: UHRF1 is a chromatin-binding protein essential for maintaining DNA methylation and histone modification states, yet its integrated role in vivo remains incompletely understood. To define its function, we generated conditional Uhrf1 knockout embryonic stem cells (ESCs) and embryos. Uhrf1(-)(/)(-) ESCs exhibited near-complete loss of 5mC and 5hmC but maintained pluripotency, whereas Uhrf1-null embryos developed normally until E8.5 and then failed to develop further by E9.5, phenocopying Dnmt1 loss. Single-cell multi-omic (ME-seq) profiling of E8.5 embryos revealed impaired lineage stabilization, widespread hypomethylation, and disrupted chromatin architecture. Uhrf1 loss was associated with altered CTCF-associated chromatin signal, broad remodeling of chromatin contacts, altered cis-regulatory relationships, and reduced predicted BMP-related ligand-receptor communication, particularly within neural crest populations. These findings identify Uhrf1 as a central regulator that tightly couples DNA methylation maintenance to 3D genome organization during gastrulation, thereby, directing early lineage specification and positioning Uhrf1 as a pivotal mediator of epigenetic information transfer during early embryogenesis.

title: Lamin A regulates chromatin structure and function in cardiac myocytes in a mouse model of lamin-cardiomyopathy.
authors: Gurha, Priyatansh; Wang, Weiyue; Cathcart, Benjamin; Rouhi, Leila; Marian, Ali J
abstract: Mutations in the LMNA gene, encoding lamin A (LMNA), cause laminopathies. Cardiac involvement is common and a major cause of mortality and morbidity in laminopathies. LMNA interacts with chromatin through lamin-associated domains (LADs) and regulates gene expression. We report that LMNA deficiency increased genome-wide CTCF occupancy, predominantly outside of the constitutive LAD (cLAD) regions. CTCF occupancy was associated with increased gene expression and enrichment of double-stranded breaks (DSBs). LMNA deficiency had a modest effect on chromatin compartments but led to mergers, splitting, and shifting boundaries of one-third of the topologically associated domains (TADs) without affecting gene expression significantly. LMNA deficiency led to a gain of  approximately 600 and a loss of  approximately 1000 loops, which were associated with increased and decreased transcript levels, respectively. Reorganization of chromatin loops affected  approximately 25% of the differentially expressed genes in the LMNA-deficient cardiac myocytes. In multivariate analysis, CTCF-binding sites, chromatin loops, and cLADs were independent predictors of gene expression in the LMNA-deficient cardiac myocytes, whereas TADs and chromatin compartments were not. Thus, LMNA deficiency changes genome-wide CTCF occupancy and loop organization, which affect gene expression in cardiac myocytes. The findings provide new insights into the pathogenesis of cardiac involvement in laminopathies.

title: CTCF knockdown reduces ABCG2 expression and intracellular biliverdin accumulation in primary uterine epithelial cells of blue-shelled ducks.
authors: Wang, Dandan; Bao, Ying; Li, Bohong; Lu, Lizhi; Li, Pan; Chen, Li
abstract: The blue eggshell phenotype in ducks is an important economic trait associated with enhanced shell strength, antioxidative capacity, and storage stability. Our previous study found that blue eggshell alleles enhanced ABCG2 expression through specific binding of the transcription factor CTCF. However, the mechanisms underlying this regulatory relationship remain unclear. In this study, ABCG2 overexpression and CTCF knockdown models were established in primary uterine epithelial cells derived from blue-shelled ducks, followed by intracellular biliverdin assays and whole-genome DNA methylation sequencing. Functional assays showed that CTCF knockdown significantly reduced ABCG2 expression and intracellular biliverdin accumulation, whereas ABCG2 overexpression increased intracellular biliverdin levels, supporting a functional association between CTCF, ABCG2 expression, and biliverdin accumulation. Genome-wide methylation profiling identified differentially methylated regions (DMRs) following CTCF knockdown, which were predominantly located in intronic and intergenic regions. However, no statistically significant difference was detected in methylation levels within the ABCG2 promoter region. Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses of DMR-associated genes identified enrichment of terms centered on extracellular matrix organization, cell adhesion, and cytoskeletal regulation, with no significant enrichment of pigmentation-related or transporter pathways. These enrichment results provide exploratory insights into the molecular changes associated with CTCF knockdown, but their functional significance remains to be determined. Collectively, our findings indicate that CTCF knockdown is associated with reduced ABCG2 expression and intracellular biliverdin accumulation, while the accompanying genome-wide DNA methylation changes may represent broader molecular alterations whose specific functional roles require further investigation.

title: Interplay of diffusive and active motion governs cohesin extrusion and CTCF barrier function
abstract: Cohesin-mediated loop extrusion constitutes a crucial process for the regulation of chromosome folding and gene expression. A rapidly-growing body of in vitro experiments suggests that cohesin molecular motor activity is finely modulated by both chemical and mechanical cues, whose interplay holds important implications in living cells for development and disease. Yet, biophysical models capable of accurately and efficiently capturing the breadth of reported cohesin behaviors, along with their impacts on DNA spatio-temporal organisation, remain lacking. Here, building on multiple experimental observations of single-cohesin dynamics, we introduce a mesoscale description of cohesin based on the general framework of jump-diffusion processes. We show that the finite stall force of cohesin naturally emerges from the conjunction of active, directional extrusion moves with passive, stochastic drift. The tension-dependent competition between these two orthogonal modes of motion gives rise to highly-heterogeneous cohesin kinetics featuring extrusion, translocation, and loop slipping phases, as observed in vitro. These behaviors are predicted to depend sensitively on both buffer composition and nucleosomal content, reconciling the surprising variability of cohesin kinetics reported across experimental conditions. This jump-diffusion model (JDM) is fully parametrized using available single-molecule measurements and bridges the timescale gap between microscopic stepping events and cohesin regulator association, thus providing mechanistic insights into how CTCF impedes extrusion. Hence, the JDM quantitatively describes force-dependent extrusion in both DNA curtain assays in vitro and in the context of native chromatin for genome folding predictions in nucleo, bridging these previously disparate contexts under a unified numerical and theoretical formalism.

title: MaaD-TAD: an all-atom model of the duplicated PRAMEF/HNRNPCL chromatin domain built from sequence homology
authors: Santos JRL; MacIsaac M; Moon EB; Befus AD; Marcet-Palacios M
abstract:
In the nucleus, the placement of genes in the 3D fold of DNA affects how they function. Models of this fold use two kinds of data: contact maps constructed from Hi-C, and nucleosome maps showing where DNA is wound around nucleosomes. Over evolution, sections of the genome were copied, creating near-identical regions. Reads from these regions cannot be assigned to one copy and are discarded, leaving “void regions” in both maps. We tested MaaD-TAD, a pipeline that models topologically associating domains (TADs) at the atomic level, on the PRAMEF/HNRNPCL locus on human chromosome 1. This challenging locus spans 652 kb, with only 15% of its nucleosome positions known and most contact data missing. To test our hypothesis that copies with similar sequence lie close in space, i.e. homology as a surrogate for proximity, we constructed a map of sequence homology in place of Hi-C and used CSynth to fold it into a 3D path. We then lengthened the path to fit a chromatin fibre, and refined the model by adding cohesin complexes, which stabilize chromatin structure. Cohesin is a ring-shaped protein complex through which a loop of chromatin is threaded; the loop is commonly anchored by CTCF proteins bound on either leg. Using known databases, we placed CTCF sites in our model and joined three to their copies with cohesin rings; in each pair the sites face each other, as loop anchors do. The final model holds 3,359 nucleosomes and about 55 million atoms. Micro-C, an advanced, higher-resolution form of Hi-C, provided data on two other duplicated regions that support our hypothesis: matching copies touched 1.2 to 1.9 times more often than expected. Our approach provides a novel method to reconstruct DNA regions with absent contact data and, to our knowledge, the first all-atom model of a complete TAD.

Author summary

Inside every cell, two metres of DNA are folded into a nucleus a few thousandths of a millimetre across, and where a gene sits in this fold helps decide whether it is used. We map the fold by reading millions of short DNA fragments, but regions of the genome that were copied during evolution look the same to these methods, so their data are thrown away. We asked whether such a blank region could still be modelled. We focused on a region of human chromosome 1, 652,000 DNA letters long, that holds two families of copied genes, PRAMEF and HNRNPCL, which are switched on in the earliest stages of the human embryo. Our working idea was that copies with similar sequence lie close together in space, so we used sequence similarity in place of the missing data. We then built MaaD-TAD, a pipeline that builds a 3D model in which every atom of the DNA and every atom of its packaging proteins has a position, about 55 million atoms in all. The model shows how copied genes and their control switches could pair up, and makes predictions that experiments can test. The same pipeline also builds models from measured maps.

title: Chromatin accessibility predictions reveal lineage-structured effects of noncoding variants across hematopoiesis
abstract:
Background:

Noncoding variants account for over 90% of genome-wide association study (GWAS) findings, but their mechanisms are often unclear. Sequence-to-function models provide one approach to variant interpretation by predicting the effects of genetic variation on molecular phenotypes. ChromBPNet predicts variant effects on chromatin accessibility, but how these predictions are organized across differentiation hierarchies and relate to orthogonal predictions remains unclear. Results. We trained ChromBPNet models for 17 hematopoietic cell types and scored 302,830 variants. Of 242,307 variants accessible in at least one cell type, 5.6% were predicted to alter chromatin accessibility. Variants active in more cell types had larger predicted effects. Predicted effects also reflected hematopoietic lineage structure, with sharing declining with lineage distance while effect direction was preserved in 99.6% of parent-child comparisons. ChromBPNet predictions agreed with GWAS fine-mapping but largely identified distinct variants. Fine-mapping-only variants were enriched for coding and transcript-associated variation, whereas ChromBPNet-only variants were enriched for regulatory elements, accessible chromatin, and trait-relevant activity. In K562 CRISPRi datasets, predicted accessibility gain showed limited association with target-gene validation. Regulatory elements containing CTCF motifs were less likely to have validated target genes, consistent with a role in chromatin organization rather than gene activation. Conclusions. ChromBPNet and fine-mapping provide complementary information about variant function. Predicted accessibility effects identify the cell types in which noncoding variants are likely to act and capture relationships across the hematopoietic hierarchy, but provide limited information about the genes they regulate. All predictions are available at: https://bloodnnet.ccbr.utoronto.ca/.
